statement: In matrix form, the principal element s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_n of the reflection system (W, S, B) can be written as -U^{-1}U^T where U_{i,j} = B(e_i, e_j) if j > i; B(e_i, e_j)/2 if i = j; 0 if i > j.
proof: Note that U = [L_i^T, X_i; 0, V_i] where L_i is an i \times i block such that L_i = [L_{i-1}, 0; -a_i, 1] and V_i is an (n - i) \times (n - i) block such that V_i = [1, -b_i; 0, V_{i+1}]. We now show that U s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_i = [-L_i, 0; 0, V_i] for all i. We proceed by induction. If i = 0 then there is nothing to prove. Assuming true for i - 1 we have that U s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_{i-1} s_i = [-L_{i-1}, 0; 0, V_{i-1}][I_{i-1}, 0, 0; a_i, -1, b_i; 0, 0, I_{n-i}] = [-L_{i-1}, 0, 0; 0, 1, -b_i; 0, 0, V_i][I_{i-1}, 0, 0; a_i, -1, b_i; 0, 0, I_{n-i}] = [-L_{i-1}, 0, 0; a_i, -1, -0; 0, 0, V_i] = [-L_i, 0; 0, V_i]. So we have that U s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_i = [-L_i, 0; 0, V_i] for all i, in the case that i = n we have L_n = U and that U(s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_n) = -U^T so that s_1 s_2 s_3 \cdots s_n = -U^{-1}U^T.
lean_notes: Proved in full generality via prefix induction howlett_prefix_invariant.

statement: There exists an infinite family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems which do not satisfy the Deletion Property.
proof: To obtain a family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems which fail to satisfy the Deletion Property we construct the following sequence of mixed-sign Coxeter graphs. Let \Gamma_3:= \widetilde{A}_{-2}, let \Gamma_4:= \widetilde{A}_{-2} \ast_{r_3} \{r_4\} and for n > 4 define \Gamma_n:= \Gamma_{n-1} \ast_{r_{n-1}} \{r_n\}. Each of these mixed-sign Coxeter groups contain the same relation in the above example, and fail to satisfy the Deletion Property in the same way as in the example above. More families can be constructed in a similar manner, in fact, if \Gamma is a graph and \Gamma contains \widetilde{A}_{-2} then W(\Gamma) contains the three generators associated to \widetilde{A}_{-2} and the word will appear in the associated mixed-sign Coxeter group.
lean_notes: Also proved for the block-extended family in CyclesAndDeletion.lean (theorem_1_2_infinite_family); ParabolicTransfer proves failure for every graph containing ~A_{-2}.

statement: There exists an infinite family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems which are not conjugate to a classical Coxeter system.
proof: By Theorem 3.9 a reflection system (W, S, B) is a classical Coxeter system if and only if it does not satisfy the Deletion Property. Since the family of mixed-sign Coxeter systems above do not have the Deletion Property by 1.6, then they cannot be classical Coxeter systems.
lean_notes: Combined with ClassicalCoxeterDeletion.lean (theorem_3_9_classical_iff_deletion), proves the infinite family is not O-conjugate to any classical Coxeter system.

statement: If \Gamma is a bipartite reflection diagram then (W, S, B(\Gamma)) is conjugate to (W, S, B(\Gamma_{-})) by an element of \mathcal{O}.
proof: We will use the bipartite ordering on \Gamma from Remark 2.42 and Figure 2.2. B(\Gamma) = [\Delta^{(1)}, B_*; (B_*)^T, \Delta^{(2)}]. Notice the bilinear form of the bipartite ordering of \Gamma_{-} is B(\Gamma_{-}) = [-\Delta^{(1)}, B_*; (B_*)^T, -\Delta^{(2)}]. Let P = [-I_{n_1}, 0; 0, I_{n_1+n_2}] where I_q is the q \times q identity matrix. Notice again we have P^{-1} = P = P^T. Then P^{-1} B(\Gamma) P = [-I_{n_1}, 0; 0, I_{n_1+n_2}][\Delta^{(1)}, B_*; (B_*)^T, \Delta^{(2)}][-I_{n_1}, 0; 0, I_{n_1+n_2}] = [\Delta^{(1)}, -B_*; -(B_*)^T, \Delta^{(2)}] = -B(\Gamma_{-}). This shows that P^T B(\Gamma) P = -B(\Gamma_{-}). We use Lemma 2.32 to obtain that the two reflection systems are conjugate.
lean_notes: Proves P^T * B(Gamma) * P = -B(Gamma_-) and conjugation of all generating reflections by P in O.

statement: If \Gamma is a bipartite mixed-sign Coxeter diagram then (W, S, B(\Gamma)) is conjugate to (W, S, B(\Gamma_{-})) by an element of \mathcal{O}.
lean_notes: Specialization of Theorem 1.4 to MixedSignCoxeterGraph.

statement: For even n, the reflection systems (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-n})) and (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_n)) are not conjugate reflection systems.
proof: First the bilinear form for \widetilde{A}_{-n} with n even is always negative definite as the signature is (0, n, 0). The bilinear form B(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) has the form B(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) = [-2, -1, 0, 0, \cdots, -1; -1, -2, -1, 0, \cdots, 0; 0, -1, \ddots, -1, \cdots, 0; \ldots, \ldots, \ddots, \ddots, \ddots, \ldots; -1, 0, \cdots, \cdots, -1, -2]. Let B_n = -B(\widetilde{A}_{-n}). We will use Sylvesters criterion. We show that -B_n is positive definite. The determinant of the upper k \times k corner of B_n is k+1, additionally the determinant of B_n is 4. This implies that B_n is positive definite for all n. This, in turn, implies that B(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) is negative definite for all n. Since B(\widetilde{A}_n) is positive semi-definite we conclude that B(\widetilde{A}_n) and B(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) cannot be conjugate, let alone conjugate by an orthogonal transformation. Therefore, the reflection systems are not conjugate.
lean_notes: Proves B(~A_n) is positive semidefinite degenerate while B(~A_{-n}) is strictly negative definite for even n, so they are not O-conjugate. TildeAminusEvenIso.lean further proves W(~A_{-n}) ≅ W(D_{n+1}) for all even n >= 2 and infinity of W(~A_{-n}) for all odd n >= 3.

statement: There exists a bipartite mixed-sign Coxeter system with a bipartite principal element which does not have the smallest spectral radius among other principal elements in the mixed-sign Coxeter system.
lean_notes: Witnessed by Example 3.33 (6-node bipartite graph) and also by the smaller 4-node alternating square in AlternatingSquare.lean (alternatingSquare_bipartite_not_min).

statement: A bilinear form is a function, f: \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R} such that for all u, v, w \in \mathbb{R}^n and for all c \in \mathbb{R} then f(cv, u) = cf(v, u) = f(v, cu); f(v + w, u) = f(v, u) + f(w, u); f(v, u + w) = f(v, u) + f(v, w).
lean_notes: Standard linear algebra definition; in Lean/Mathlib bilinear forms are represented by LinearMap.BilinForm or real matrices Matrix (Fin n) (Fin n) R.

statement: A bilinear form is symmetric if f(v, u) = f(u, v) for all v, u \in \mathbb{R}^n. The matrix B is used to define a symmetric bilinear form on \mathbb{R}^n. For any v, u \in \mathbb{R}^n we have B(v, u) = v^T B u where v^T is the transpose of v. We will use V to denote \mathbb{R}^n with the bilinear form B.
lean_notes: Symmetric bilinear form represented by a symmetric matrix B with B_symm : B.IsSymm.

statement: The vectors v and u are orthogonal relative to B if B(v, u) = 0. Let H_v:= \{u \in V \mid B(v, u) = 0\} be the set of all vectors u which are orthogonal to v relative to B.
lean_notes: Orthogonality relative to B is expressed directly as B i j = 0 or dotProduct v (B *ᵥ u) = 0.

statement: For every v \in V the map s_v: V \to V defined by s_v(u):= u - \frac{2B(u, v)}{B(v, v)} v is a reflection through H_v on V. The map s_v is a reflection in the sense that s_v is linear; negates the vector v (s_v(v) = -v); pointwise fixes H_v (if u \in H_v then s_v(u) = u); is an involution (s_v^2(u) = u for all u \in V). We will use the basis \Pi_+ of \mathbb{R}^n to define a set of distinguished generators for a group acting on V. For each basis element e_i define the map s_{e_i}(v):= v - \frac{2B(v, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i.
lean_notes: Matrix form of generating reflections s_{e_i}, together with linearity, negation of e_i, and involution.

statement: We will often use s_i in place of s_{e_i}. Notice that each generating reflection is defined to be an element of the orthogonal group on V (s_i \in O(V) for all i).
lean_notes: Verifies each s_i preserves B (i.e. s_i in O(V)).

statement: Not only does s_i leave H_{e_i} fixed, the action of s_i on a vector v \in V only changes the ith coordinate of v. Suppose that v = \sum_{j=1}^{n} v_j e_j with v_j \in \mathbb{R} then s_i(v) = v - \frac{2B(v, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = \sum_j v_j e_j - \frac{2B(\sum_j v_j e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = \sum_j v_j e_j - 2\sum_j v_j \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i. So the kth coordinate of v is then (s_i(v))_k = v_k if k \ne i; v_k - 2\sum_j v_j \frac{B(e_j, e_k)}{B(e_k, e_k)} if k = i (2.6.1).
lean_notes: Explicit coordinate-wise action of s_i on a vector v; see also ReflectionSystem.lean (reflectionMatrix_apply).

statement: Each s_i \in S is thought of as an n \times n matrix in \mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{R}) s_i = [s_i(e_1), s_i(e_2), \ldots, s_i(e_n)] where by equation 2.6.1 we know that s_i(e_j) is the column vector which has a 1 in the jth component and -\frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} in the ith component.
lean_notes: Defines s_i directly as an n x n matrix with entries delta_{kj} - 2 B_{ij}/B_{ii} for k = i.

statement: We use \mathcal{O} for the subgroup of O(V) which fixes the set \{\pm e_1, \pm e_2, \pm e_3, \ldots, \pm e_n\}.
lean_notes: Signed permutation matrices permuting {±e_1, ..., ±e_n}.

statement: The set S = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\} is the set of generating reflections.
lean_notes: Generating reflection family i ↦ reflectionMatrix S.B i.

statement: Let W = \langle s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n \rangle be the reflection group generated by S.
lean_notes: Submonoid / subgroup generated by the generating reflections s_i.

statement: The reflection group W is generated by matrices which are orthogonal reflections, therefore W is a subgroup of the orthogonal group on V. (W \subset O(V)).
lean_notes: Embeds W faithfully into GL_n(R) preserving the bilinear form B.

statement: The set of roots of a reflection system is defined to be \Phi:= W\Pi_+ = \{w e_i \mid w \in W\}.
lean_notes: Defines Phi = {w e_i | w in W} as ReflectionSystem.roots with W-invariance, negation closure, non-vanishing, and quadratic-form invariance.

statement: A vector v is positive if v \ne 0 and v = \sum_i v_i e_i and v_i \ge 0 for all i. Let \Phi_+ be the set of roots which are positive, we call these positive roots.
lean_notes: Nonzero vector with all coordinates >= 0.

statement: We say the group W preserves the bilinear form B if for all w \in W and for all v, u \in V we have B(wv, wu) = B(v, u). Since W is generated by S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n\} then any element in w \in W may be written in terms of generators in the letters of S.
lean_notes: Bilinear-form invariance w^T * B * w = B for all w in W.

statement: When w is written in terms of generating reflections we call any such representation a word representation of w in the letters of S. A word representation for a given element in W is not unique. For instance, the identity element has infinitely many different word representations in the letters of S, 1 = (s_i s_i)^n for every n \in \mathbb{N}. Note this also implies that any element of W has infinitely many word representations.
lean_notes: Evaluation of a word (List (Fin n)) in the generating reflections.

statement: The length of w is the smallest k such that w can be written in terms of k letters in S, such a representation is a reduced word representation of w in the letters of S. We use the notation l(w) = k to denote that the reduced length of w is k. By convention, l(1) = 0. If l(w) = k then there are n^k possibilities for a reduced word representation of w.
lean_notes: Reduced word predicate; minimum word length function len is also defined in RootPositivity.lean (line 88) and MathlibDraft/GeometricRep.lean (geomLen).

statement: The reflection group W preserves the bilinear form B.
proof: First we show that each of the generators s_i of W will preserve the bilinear form. Let c_1 = B(v, e_i), c_2 = B(u, e_i) and k = \frac{2}{B(e_i, e_i)} then B(s_i(v), s_i(u)) = B[v - kB(v, e_i)e_i, u - kB(u, e_i)e_i] = B(v - kc_1 e_i, u - kc_2 e_i) = B(v, u - kc_2 e_i) - kc_1 B(e_i, u - kc_2 e_i) = B(v, u) - kc_2 B(v, e_i) - kc_1 B[e_i, u - kc_2 e_i] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - kc_1 [B(e_i, u) - kc_2 B(e_i, e_i)] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - kc_1 [kc_2 - 2kc_2] = B(v, u) - k^2 c_2 c_1 - k^2 c_1 c_2 + 2k^2 c_2 c_1 = B(v, u). Now consider any w \in W. Recall, by Definition 2.15 w is a product of the generating reflections say, w = \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)}. Repeated applications of the above computation gives B(wv, wu) = B(\prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} v, \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} u) = B(v, u). So we may conclude the group W preserves the bilinear form B.
lean_notes: Generator case proved in ReflectionSystem.lean (reflectionMatrix_preserves_B); extended to all w in W.

statement: A reflection system on \mathbb{R}^n is the triple (W, S, B); where B is a symmetric bilinear form, S = \{s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots, s_n\} where the action of s_i on e_j is s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i is the set of generating reflections thought of as the matrices in Remark 2.7, and W is the reflection group generated by S.
lean_notes: Core structure packaging symmetric matrix B with nonzero diagonal.

statement: Throughout, we assume that the vector space V is \mathbb{R}^n with the bilinear form B. Since the set of generating reflections are defined with respect to \Pi_+ and B, we can recover the set of generating reflections S given the matrix B. Therefore, we may refer to the set of generators by S(B). Since the group W is generated by S, we can also recover the reflection group W from B and we use W(B) to refer to the reflection group which preserves the bilinear form B.
lean_notes: Notation convention S(B), W(B); realized by taking ReflectionSystem as the primary object.

statement: Since each s_i is a reflection we have s_i^2 = 1 \in W.
lean_notes: Each generating reflection satisfies s_i * s_i = 1.

statement: If \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} is a reduced word representation for w in the letters of S and k is odd then w cannot be the identity element in W.
proof: Since each generator is an involution, for each i define the map det(s_i):= -1. Now extend det to a homomorphism det: W \to \{\pm 1\}. Recall suppose that \prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)} is a reduced word representation of w in the letters of S then det(w) = det(\prod_{j=1}^{k} s_{\sigma(j)}) = \prod_{i=1}^{k} det(s_{\sigma(i)}) = (-1)^k. Namely, we have shown that if a given word representation of w in the letters of S has odd length then det(w) = -1. Since det(1) = 1 and det a homomorphism then w cannot be the identity element in W.
lean_notes: Proved via det(s_i) = -1 (det_reflectionMatrix) and det(wordProd w) = (-1)^w.length.

statement: If e_i and e_j are orthogonal relative to B then s_i and s_j commute. That is, if B(e_i, e_j) = 0 then s_i s_j = s_j s_i.
proof: Let v \in V and let \alpha = \frac{2B(e_i, v)}{B(e_i, e_i)} and \beta = \frac{2B(e_j, v)}{B(e_j, e_j)} then s_i(s_j(v)) = s_i(v - \beta e_j) = v - \beta e_j - \frac{2B(v - \beta e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i + 2\beta \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i = v - \beta e_j - \alpha e_i + 2\alpha \frac{B(e_j, e_i)}{B(e_j, e_j)} e_j = v - \alpha e_i - \frac{2B(v - \alpha e_i, e_j)}{B(e_j, e_j)} e_j = s_j(v - \alpha e_i) = s_j s_i(v).
lean_notes: If B i j = 0 then s_i * s_j = s_j * s_i.

statement: A reflection diagram \Gamma with n nodes is an undirected graph with nodes denoted by r_i with weights weight(r_i). The edge weight between r_i and r_j is denoted by weight(r_i, r_j). If there is no edge connecting r_i to r_j then weight(r_i, r_j) = 0.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: SimpleGraph adjacency of a reflection diagram; node and edge weights are carried by the symmetric matrix B.

statement: Given a reflection diagram \Gamma we define a symmetric bilinear form B(\Gamma) by B(\Gamma)(e_i, e_j) = weight(r_i) if i = j; weight(r_i, r_j) if i \ne j. Similarly, given a bilinear form B we define a reflection diagram \Gamma(B).
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Constructs B(Gamma) from a weighted MixedSignCoxeterGraph; general reflection diagrams are identified with their symmetric matrix B.

statement: If B is a symmetric bilinear form on \mathbb{R}^n then let \Gamma(B) be the reflection diagram with n nodes r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_n defined as follows. Define weight(r_i) to be B(e_i, e_i). If B(e_i, e_j) = 0 then there is no edge between r_i and r_j, otherwise define weight(r_i, r_j) to be B(e_i, e_j).
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Underlying SimpleGraph Gamma(B) with edges where i != j and B i j != 0.

statement: Given a bilinear form B, the reflection diagram \Gamma(B) determines a bilinear form B(\Gamma(B)), which is easily seen to be B. Similarly given a reflection diagram \Gamma, the bilinear form defined by \Gamma is B(\Gamma) and the reflection diagram of this bilinear form is \Gamma.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Expository remark on the correspondence between B and Gamma(B).

statement: Let (W, S, B) be a reflection system. We define S(B) to be the set of generating reflections for W(B) the reflection group in the reflection system (W, S, B). Similarly, we define S(\Gamma) to be the set of generating reflections for W(\Gamma) the reflection group in the reflection system (W, S, B(\Gamma)).
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Notation convention for S(B), W(B), S(Gamma), W(Gamma).

statement: If node e_i is not connected to node e_j then s_i s_j = s_j s_i.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
proof: Since node e_i is not connected to node e_j then B(e_i, e_j) = 0 and we may use Proposition 2.22.
lean_notes: Direct corollary of Proposition 2.22 for non-adjacent nodes.

statement: Two reflection systems (W_1, S_1, B_1) and (W_2, S_2, B_2) are conjugate if there is an orthogonal transformation P \in \mathcal{O} with B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P, S_2 = \pm P^T S_1 P, and W_2 = \pm P^T W_1 P. Recall the involution s_i is defined with respect to \Pi_+ = \{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_n\} and a symmetric bilinear form, s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B(e_i, e_j)}{B(e_i, e_i)} e_i. The set \mathcal{O} is precisely the set of elements in the orthogonal group which permute \pm\Pi_+.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Conjugacy of reflection systems via P in O (SignedPerm).

statement: Recall if P \in \mathcal{O} then it is an element of the orthogonal group, specifically P has the property that P^T = P = P^{-1}.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Proves P^T * P = 1 for all P in O. (Note: P = P^T holds for symmetric P such as bipartiteConjugator, not for non-involutive permutations.)

statement: For every symmetric bilinear form B, we have W(B) = W(-B).
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
proof: Let B_1 = B and let B_2 = -B. Let S_1 = \{s_i\} be the set of generating reflections for W(B_1) and S_2 = \{s'_i\} is the set of generating reflections for W(B_2). Recall that s_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B_1(e_i, e_j)}{B_1(e_i, e_i)} e_i and that s'_i(e_j) = e_j - \frac{2B_2(e_i, e_j)}{B_2(e_i, e_i)} e_i. Now, notice since -B_1 = B_2 we notice that \frac{B_1(v, u)}{B_1(x, y)} = \frac{B_2(v, u)}{B_2(x, y)} for all v, u, x, y \in V. We conclude that s_i = s'_i so that each of the generators for W_1 and W_2 are equal, so the generators will generate the same reflection group. We can conclude that W_1 = W_2.
lean_notes: Proves reflectionMatrix (-B) i = reflectionMatrix B i, so S(-B) = S(B) and W(-B) = W(B).

statement: Suppose B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P where P \in \mathcal{O} then (W_1, S_1, B_1) and (W_2, S_2, B_2) are conjugate reflection systems.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
proof: Let P \in \mathcal{O} with B_2 = \pm P^T B_1 P. Consider e_i, e_j \in V_2 then B_2(e_i, e_j) = \pm e_i^T B_2 e_j = \pm e_i^T P^T B_1 P e_j = \pm B_1(P e_i, P e_j). That is that B_2 is obtained by a change of basis on \pm B_1 with e_i replaced by P e_i = \pm e_j. Suppose that S_1 = \{s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n\} and S_2 = \{s'_1, s'_2, \ldots, s'_m\}. Recall that the s_i (and s'_i) are defined with respect to e_i. Since P is an orthogonal transformation we know that n = m, and furthermore since P \in \mathcal{O} then P^T s_i P = \pm s'_j for some s'_j \in S_2. Since each of the generators are conjugate by an orthogonal transformation we can further deduce that W_1 and W_2 are conjugate, and therefore isomorphic groups.
lean_notes: Both + and - sign cases proved for P in O.

statement: An isomorphism of graphs is a map \varphi: \Gamma_1 \to \Gamma_2 with the following properties: 1. For every node r_i \in Node \Gamma_1 we have \varphi(r_i) \in Node \Gamma_2. 2. For every node r'_i \in Node \Gamma_2 we have \varphi^{-1}(r'_i) \in Node \Gamma_1. 3. If node r_i is weighted with B(e_i, e_i) then node \varphi(r_i) also has weight B(e_i, e_i). 4. If B(e_i, e_j) is the edge weight between r_i and r_j, then B(e_i, e_j) also is the edge weight between \varphi(r_i) and \varphi(r_j).
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Weight-preserving bijection between reflection diagrams.

statement: Suppose that \varphi: \Gamma_1 \to \Gamma_2 is an isomorphism of graphs then \varphi induces an element \sigma of the symmetric group which acts on n letters where n is the number of nodes in \Gamma as follows. If \varphi(r_i) = r'_j then \sigma(i) = j.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Graph isomorphism is parameterized directly by a permutation sigma : Equiv.Perm (Fin n).

statement: An isomorphism of reflection diagrams induces an isomorphism of reflection groups. The converse is not true, in general. The reflection diagram gives us more information than just the abstract group; it gives the triple (W, S, B). This is a more restrictive requirement than an isomorphism of groups, as seen in the following example.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
lean_notes: Expository remark contrasting diagram isomorphism with abstract group isomorphism.

statement: The reflection diagram will explicitly determine a set of generators and a presentation for a reflection group. Sometimes different choices of generators will determine non-isomorphic reflection diagrams. We give one example here, consider D_8 the group of reflections and rotations which leave a square centered at the origin unchanged. Here we compare three presentations of D_8. (D_8, S_1, B_1) \langle s_1, s_2 \mid s_1^2 = s_2^2 = (s_1 s_2)^4 = 1 \rangle (D_8, S_2, B_2) \langle s_1, s_2, s_3, s_4 \mid s_i^2 = 1 \forall i, (s_1 s_2)^4 = (s_1 s_3)^2 = 1, (s_1 s_4)^4 = (s_2 s_3)^4 = (s_2 s_4)^2 = (s_3 s_4)^4 = 1 \rangle (D_8, S_3, B_3) \langle r, s \mid s^2 = r^4 = (s r)^2 = 1 \rangle Notice that the presentation associated to (D_8, S_3, B_3) has two generators r, s. However since r is not an involution, (D_8, S_3, B_3) is not a reflection system. The other two presentations (D_8, S_1, B_1) and (D_8, S_2, B_2) both happen to be reflection systems; in fact they are both classical Coxeter systems. The may be thought of matrix groups generated by matrices for S. For instance, B_1 is 2 \times 2 matrix below, and B_2 is the 4 \times 4 matrix below B_1 = [2, -1; -1, 2] B_2 = [2, -\sqrt{2}, 0, -\sqrt{2}; -\sqrt{2}, 2, -\sqrt{2}, 0; 0, -\sqrt{2}, 2, -\sqrt{2}; -\sqrt{2}, 0, -\sqrt{2}, 2]. An inspection of the reflection diagrams in Figure 2.1 shows that the corresponding graphs are not isomorphic. Furthermore the reflection systems are not conjugate since (for instance) B_1 is a 2 \times 2 matrix whereas B_2 is a 4 \times 4 matrix.

statement: If \Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2 then B(\Gamma_1) is conjugate to B(\Gamma_2) by an element of \mathcal{O}.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
proof: Assume \Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2 by a map \varphi. Since the graphs are isomorphic by Remark 2.34 there is a permutation \sigma. We identify \sigma with a map on the standard basis elements. Let P^{-1} = [\sigma(e_1), \sigma(e_2), \ldots, \sigma(e_n)] then P \in \mathcal{O} and P is the change of basis between B(\Gamma_1) and B(\Gamma_2); that is P conjugates B(\Gamma_1) to B(\Gamma_2).
lean_notes: Graph isomorphism induces P in O conjugating B(Gamma_1) to B(Gamma_2).

statement: The graphs \Gamma_1 and \Gamma_2 are isomorphic if and only if (W, S, B(\Gamma_1)) and (W, S, B(\Gamma_2)) are conjugate reflection systems.
section: 2.3 Conjugate reflection systems and reflection diagrams
proof: If \Gamma_1 \cong \Gamma_2 then we use Lemma 2.37. If the reflection systems are conjugate this follows because \mathcal{O} is just a relabeling of s_i's and therefore the graphs differ by a relabeling of the nodes.
lean_notes: Proves equivalence for permutation-matrix conjugacy and invariance of diagonal/absolute off-diagonal entries under O.

statement: Note, that P needs to be in \mathcal{O} otherwise Corollary 2.38 is not true. For instance, every symmetric n \times n matrix B is conjugate to a diagonal matrix of it's eigenvalues. The reflection diagram for a diagonal matrix would consist of n nodes, all disjoint. The two corresponding graphs may not be isomorphic.

Suppose that the nodes in N_1 are r_1, r_2, \ldots, r_{n_1} and the nodes in N_2 are numbered r_{n_1+1}, r_{n_1+2}, \ldots, r_{n_1+n_2}. statement: We say a reflection system is irreducible if the associated graph is connected.
lean_notes: Connectedness via reflexive-transitive closure of B u v != 0.

statement: Suppose \Gamma is comprised of exactly two connected components \Gamma_1 and \Gamma_2, then B(\Gamma) is reducible and W(\Gamma) \cong W(\Gamma_1) \times W(\Gamma_2).
proof: Suppose that \Gamma_1 and \Gamma_2 are two connected components of \Gamma. Label the nodes of \Gamma_1 by 1, 2, 3, \ldots, n_1 and the nodes of \Gamma_2 by r_{n_1+1}, r_{n_1+2}, \ldots, r_{n_1+n_2}. Let V_1 = \mathrm{Span}\{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_{n_1}\}, V_2 = \mathrm{Span}\{e_{n_1+1}, e_{n_1+2} \ldots, e_{n_1+n_2}\}, and V = \mathrm{Span}\{e_1, e_2, \ldots, e_{n_1+n_2}\}. Let W_1 = \langle s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n_1} \rangle, W_2 = \langle s_{n_1+1}, s_{n_1+2}, s_{n_1+3}, \ldots, s_{n_1+n_2} \rangle and W = \langle s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_{n_1+n_2} \rangle. If r_i \in \Gamma_1 and r_j \in \Gamma_2 then notice that B(e_i, e_j) = 0 therefore B has the form B = [B_1, 0; 0, B_2]. So we see that B is reducible. We will show that W \cong W_1 \times W_2. Furthermore, W_1 pointwise fixes V_2 and W_2 pointwise fixes V_1. Let w \in W and consider any word representation of w in the letters of S say \sum_{j=1}^k s_{\sigma(j)}. We notice that if r_i \in \mathrm{Node}(\Gamma_1) and r_j \in \mathrm{Node}(\Gamma_2) then since r_i and r_j are not connected that s_j s_i = s_i s_j. More explicitly we may rearrange the letters so that generators of W(\Gamma_1) always appear to the left of generators of W(\Gamma_2), however in doing this we have a decomposition of w in terms of (letters in S_1)(letters in S_2). Thus we have W \cong W_1 \times W_2. Additionally, suppose w_1 \in W_1 and u \in V_2 then u = \sum_j u_j e_j where u_j \in \mathbb{R} and j \in \mathrm{Node}(\Gamma_2). Then w_1 u = w_1(\sum_j u_j e_j) = \sum_j u_j w_1 e_j = \sum_j u_j e_j = u so we have that u \in H_{w_1}. Since w_1 was chosen arbitrarily from W_1 we can conclude that W_1 pointwise fixes V_2. A similar argument shows that W_2 pointwise fixes V_1.
lean_notes: Proves every word factors into commuting component words and each component pointwise fixes the complementary subspace.

statement: If \Gamma is comprised of exactly k connected components \Gamma_1, \Gamma_2, \cdots, \Gamma_k then W(\Gamma) \cong W(\Gamma_1) \times W(\Gamma_2) \times \cdots \times W(\Gamma_k).
lean_notes: Proves full k-component word factorization and explicit group isomorphism W(Gamma) ≃* ∀ c : Fin k, W(Gamma_c).

statement: The signature of a bilinear form is defined to be \mathrm{sig}(B) = (p, q, l) where p is the number of positive eigenvalues of B, q is the number of negative eigenvalues of B, and l = n - (p + q).
lean_notes: Eigenvalue signature triple sig(B) = (p, q, l) via Matrix.IsHermitian.eigenvalues with p + q + l = n and definiteness equivalences.

statement: The quadratic form associated to a bilinear form is Q(v) = B(v, v).
lean_notes: Quadratic form quadForm B v = v^T B v.

statement: For all w \in W and v \in V we have Q(w \cdot v) = B(w \cdot v, w \cdot v) = B(v, v) = Q(v) so that the group W preserves the set of \{v \in V: |Q(v)| = c\} where c \in \mathbb{R}.
lean_notes: Invariance of Q(v) follows directly from w^T * B * w = B.

statement: A real-valued symmetric bilinear form is positive definite when Q(v) \ge 0 with Q(v) = 0 if and only if v = 0. When B is positive definite then the bilinear form may be used to define an inner product on \mathbb{R}^n. In order for this to occur, B must have all positive eigenvalues. In this case, Q(v) can be used to define a norm on vectors, \sqrt{Q(v)}. Furthermore, the bilinear form may be used to define an angle measurement between two vectors v, w as \mathrm{angle}(v, w) = B(v, w)/\sqrt{Q(v)Q(w)}. When B is positive definite Remark 2.49 says that the action of the reflection group W on V "preserves" lengths of vectors and pairwise angle measurements. However, some of the bilinear forms that we examine do not define an inner product space. In fact, Example 3.16 has signature (1, 1, 0). The existence of a negative eigenvalue ensures the existence of a v \in V with Q(v) < 0.
lean_notes: Defines positive definiteness and indefiniteness and verifies indefinite example A_2(+,-).

statement: Given an irreducible reflection system (W, S, B) with reflection diagram \Gamma which has n nodes we will classify the system as: 1. Spherical if \mathrm{sig}(B) = (n, 0, 0) or \mathrm{sig}(V, B) = (0, n, 0). 2. Affine if \mathrm{sig}(B) = (n - 1, 0, 1) or \mathrm{sig}(V, B) = (0, n - 1, 1). 3. Hyperbolic if \mathrm{sig}(B) = (n - 1, 1, 0) or \mathrm{sig}(V, B) = (1, n - 1, 0). 4. Higher-rank otherwise.
lean_notes: Full 4-way classification (spherical, affine, hyperbolic, higherRank) explicitly separating hyperbolic from higher-rank indefinite systems.

statement: For instance, if a bilinear form is spherical then W preserves the set \{v \in V | Q|(v)| = c\} with c > 0. This set is homeomorphic to S^{n-1}.
lean_notes: Verifies positive definiteness of A_2(+,+) and indefiniteness of A_2(+,-).

statement: A principal element is an element of the reflection group W, containing exactly one of each of the generators of the reflection group W. Specifically, a principal element has the form w_\sigma = s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} where \sigma is a permutation of 1, 2, 3, \ldots, n.
lean_notes: Ordered principal element s_0 ... s_{n-1}; general permutation principal words defined in TreeConjugacy.lean (IsPrincipalWord).

statement: In a reflection group W there are between 1 and n! principal elements.
lean_notes: Elementary counting remark (between 1 and n! principal elements).

statement: Let \Gamma \ast_{r_i}^m \{r_t\} be the graph obtained by adding the node r_t by an edge with weight m to node r_i in \Gamma.
lean_notes: Tail-join construction for Gamma_n = Gamma_{n-1} *_{r_{n-1}} {r_n}; general subdiagram inclusion modeled via arbitrary embeddings f : Fin m -> Fin n.

statement: Let \Gamma/(r_i) denote the graph obtained by deleting node r_i and adjacent edges from the graph \Gamma.
lean_notes: Node deletion Gamma / (r_i) via Matrix.submatrix with Fin.succAbove i and parabolic relation transfer.

statement: Notice the notion for the join and the deletion of a node. The joining of a node to a graph will change the reflection group by an amalgamated product. Similarly, the removal of node r_i and adjacent edges will add the relation s_i = 1 to the presentation of the reflection group.
lean_notes: Expository remark on amalgamated products and quotient relations.

statement: Suppose that \Gamma is a reflection diagram which is a tree, then all of the principal elements of W(\Gamma) are in the same conjugacy class.
proof: The proof is by induction on the number of nodes of \Gamma. If \Gamma has a single node r_1 then there is only one principal element in the reflection group W. If we add a node to r_1 then we have \Gamma \ast_{r_1}^m \{r_t\} has two nodes, and there are two distinct principal elements s_1 s_2 and s_2 s_1 notice that a conjugation by s_1 (or s_2) shows that these elements are in the same conjugacy class. Now consider any principal element in W(\Gamma) where \Gamma is a tree with n nodes. Assume all the principal elements are in the same conjugacy class, say w_\sigma = s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)}. Suppose s_t is now placed anywhere in the above word. There are two cases to consider, either s_t is placed to the left of s_i or to the right of s_i. Recall that only r_i is connected to t, this means if s_t is placed to the right of s_i then s_t may be moved to the far right of the word by repeated uses of Proposition 2.28, so in this case the principal element is equal to w_\sigma = s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} s_t. On the other hand, if s_t appears to the left of s_i repeated applications of Proposition 2.28 yield s_t s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} recalling that each reflection is an involution we can now conjugate by s_t s_t s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} = s_t s_t s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} s_t = s_{\sigma(1)} s_{\sigma(2)} \cdots s_{\sigma(n)} s_t = w_\sigma so the two elements are in the same conjugacy class.
lean_notes: Full proof for arbitrary forests/trees via combinatorial commutation/cyclic-shift moves; leaf step also in ComponentsAndTrees.lean (leaf_insert_conj).

statement: In [Shi01], Coxeter graphs are used to study the conjugacy classes of Coxeter elements using Coxeter graphs. Similarly, [MM08] gives a formula which uses the Coxeter graph to calculate the number of conjugacy classes of Coxeter elements. These methods might be extended and generalized to study the number of conjugacy classes of principal elements in a reflection group.
lean_notes: Open question in thesis; Lean proves C_4(+,-,+,-) has at least two distinct conjugacy classes of principal elements (traces -8 and -7).

statement: A principal polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of the matrix representation of a principal element w_\sigma denoted by \chi(w_\sigma, x).
lean_notes: Uses Mathlib Matrix.charpoly for the principal polynomial.

statement: Suppose that \lambda_i are the eigenvalues of a matrix representation of w then the spectral radius of w is defined as \max\{|\lambda_i|\}, it is denoted \lambda(w).
lean_notes: Spectral radius lambda(M) = sSup {||mu|| | HasEigenC M mu} with boundedness, nonnegativity, and upper/lower-bound theorems.

statement: Let \Lambda(\Gamma) = \min\{\lambda(w): w is a principal element in W(\Gamma)\}
lean_notes: Minimal spectral radius Lambda(Gamma); compared directly across principal elements in SpectralRadius.lean and AlternatingSquare.lean.

statement: Up to scalar multiplication, the principal polynomial is \det(Ux + U^T) where U is as in Theorem 1.1.
proof: We may use Theorem 1.1 to compute principal polynomials as follows \chi(w_\sigma, x) = \det(xI - w_\sigma) = \det(xI + U^{-1}U^T) = \det(U^{-1}) \det(Ux + U^T). Therefore, up to scalar multiplication, the principal polynomial is \det(Ux + U^T).
lean_notes: Proves det(xI - w) = det(U)^{-1} * det(xU + U^T).

statement: A polynomial f(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n a_i x^i is palindromic if a_i = a_{n-i} for i = 0, 1, \ldots n, that is the coefficients of the principal polynomial read the same forward and backward.
lean_notes: Definition of palindromic polynomial; explicit palindromic characteristic polynomials verified in SpectralRadius.lean and TwoDefectCycle.lean.

statement: For a polynomial f(x) = a_d \prod_{i=1}^n (x - \lambda_I) define the Mahler measure of f to be M(f) = |a_d| \cdot \prod_{i=1}^n \max\{1, |\lambda_i|\}. Principal polynomials arise in the study of Lehmer's problem. The first chapter of [EW99] gives a good introduction to Lehmer's problem and Mahler's measure. Lehmer's number \lambda_{\mathrm{Lehmer}} is the largest real root of the polynomial x^{10} + x^9 - x^7 - x^6 - x^5 - x^4 - x^3 + x + 1. Lehmer's problem asks the question if there exists a c > 1 such that every polynomial f with integer coefficients and M(f) > 1 has M(f) \ge c. Currently, no polynomial has been found with a smaller Mahler measure than Lehmer's number. The problem has been reduced to studying the Mahler measure of reciprocal polynomials, see [Smy] and [Hir09]. Since every principal polynomial is reciprocal, principal polynomials make good candidates to further study the problem. Lehmer's number makes an appearance in Coxeter groups as it is the minimal spectral radius of a Coxeter element in (W, S, B(E_{10})).
lean_notes: Definition of Mahler measure and discussion of Lehmer problem.

statement: A mixed-sign Coxeter system is a reflection system (W, S, B) where the bilinear form B has the following properties: B(e_i, e_i) = \delta_i 2 where \delta_i is either + or -. Here, \delta_i is the sign of node i and B(e_i, e_j) = -2\cos(\pi/m(i,j)) where m(i, j) \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \infty\}. For the case when m(i, j) = \infty we define B(e_i, e_j) = -2.
lean_notes: Full definition of mixed-sign Coxeter system with B(e_i,e_i) = ±2 and B(e_i,e_j) = -2 cos(pi/m(i,j)) or -2.

statement: A mixed-sign Coxeter graph is a reflection diagram for a mixed-sign Coxeter system.
lean_notes: Weighted graph with node signs and edge labels m(i,j) in {2,3,...,infty}.

statement: Because mixed-sign Coxeter systems always have this form we will simplify the notation in a mixed-sign Coxeter graph. Since |B(e_i, e_i)| = 2 we will use + or - for the weight of node r_i corresponding to 2 and -2 respectively. In the case where there is no label we will assume +. Since B(e_i, e_j) = -2\cos(\pi/m(i,j)) we will use m(i, j) for the weight of node m(i, j). When m(i, j) = 3 we will not label the edge with a number.
lean_notes: Diagram shorthand conventions (+, -, unlabeled edge = 3).

statement: A Coxeter system or classical Coxeter system is a reflection system (W, S, B) where the bilinear form B has the following properties: B_{i,i} = 2; B_{i,j} = -2\cos(\pi/m(i,j)) where m(i, j) \in \{2, 3, \ldots, \infty\}. For the case when m(i, j) = \infty we define B_{i,j} = -2.

statement: A classical Coxeter system is a mixed-sign Coxeter system when all of the nodes on a mixed-sign Coxeter graph are positive.
proof: From the definition, when all of the nodes on a mixed-sign Coxeter graph are positive then B(e_i, e_i) = 2 for all i. However, this is the definition of the bilinear form in a classical Coxeter system.
lean_notes: Proves all-positive MixedSignCoxeterGraph produces the classical Coxeter bilinear form.

statement: A Coxeter graph is the mixed-sign Coxeter graph of a Coxeter system.
lean_notes: MixedSignCoxeterGraph with all node signs positive.

statement: (Deletion Property) Given an expression w = s_1 \cdots s_k with l(w) < k (that is that w is not reduced), then there exist indices 1 \le i < j \le k such that w = s_1 \cdots \hat{s}_i \cdots \hat{s}_j \cdots s_k (here hat denotes omission).
lean_notes: Deletion Property defined in ClassicalDeletion.lean and proved for every CoxeterSystem in ClassicalCoxeterDeletion.lean (deletion_of_coxeterSystem) and MathlibDraft/CoxeterDeletion.lean.

statement: (Exchange Property) Let w = s_1 s_2 \ldots s_k be a reduced expression and s \in S. If l(sw) \le l(w), then sw = s_1 \ldots \hat{s}_i \ldots s_k for some i \in \{1, 2, 3, \ldots, k\} (again, here hat denotes omission).
lean_notes: Exchange Property defined in ClassicalDeletion.lean and proved for every CoxeterSystem in ClassicalCoxeterDeletion.lean (exchange_of_coxeterSystem) and MathlibDraft/CoxeterDeletion.lean.

statement: Let (W, S, B) be a reflection system. Suppose that W is a group generated by a set of involutions S, then the following are equivalent: 1. (W, S, B) is a classical Coxeter system. 2. (W, S, B) satisfies the Deletion Property. 3. (W, S, B) has the Exchange Property.
proof: A proof of the above theorem is contained in [BB05]. A different proof using van Kampen diagrams is given in [Bah05].
lean_notes: Full 3-way equivalence proved across ClassicalDeletion.lean, CoxeterPresentation.lean, and ClassicalCoxeterDeletion.lean.

statement: If (W, S, B) is a classical Coxeter system with w \in W and s_i \in S then w(e_i) \in \Phi^+ \Leftrightarrow l(ws_i) > l(w).
section: 3.1 Root systems of rank 2 mixed-sign Coxeter systems
proof: For a proof see [BB05].

statement: Suppose (W, S, B) is a classical Coxeter system where s_1 s_2 \in W has infinite order and define w_k = (s_1 s_2)^k. Then w_k e_1 \in \Phi^+ for all k.
section: 3.1 Root systems of rank 2 mixed-sign Coxeter systems
proof: Consider the sequence of elements g_k \in W where g_1 = s_2, g_2 = s_1 s_2, g_3 = s_2 s_1 s_2, g_4 = s_1 s_2 s_1 s_2, \ldots. Notice that l(g_k s_1) > l(g_k) for all k so we conclude that g_k e_1 \in \Phi^+ for all k. Now notice that w_k is a subsequence of g_k. The result follows.
lean_notes: Proved for any rank-n reflection system and any infinite-dihedral pair (s_i, s_j) via Chebyshev sequences.

statement: Let e_1 be the positive root in the root system for A_2(-, +) in Example 3.16. There is a sequence of principal elements \{w_p\} such that w_{p+1} = s_i w_p (where i = 1 or 2, depending on k) and l(w_{p+1}) > l(w_p) and there are infinitely many p such that w_p(e_i) \notin \Phi^+
section: 3.1 Root systems of rank 2 mixed-sign Coxeter systems
proof: See Example 3.16.
lean_notes: Explicitly proves sign oscillation of the root orbit in A_2(+,-)[3].

statement: When m = 3 we have six roots in total. The roots e_1, e_2, and e_1 + e_2 are positive roots whereas, -e_1, -(e_1 + e_2), and -e_2 are negative roots. Figure 3.1.1 shows these six roots along with the set B(v, v) = 2. Figure 3.1.1 gives a geometric interpretation about the angle between e_1 and e_2 in V.

statement: This appears to also be the first example of a rank 2 hyperbolic reflection system, a reflection system (W, S, B) where sigB = (1, 1, 0).

statement: This is an explicit example of a hyperbolic rank 2 mixed-sign Coxeter system. This example shows Proposition 3.12. A comparison of the root structure here gives some intuition as to why the Deletion Property does not extend to the mixed-sign case. Consider the mixed-sign Coxeter graph A_2(+, -) in Figure 3.9. The bilinear form associated to this mixed-sign Coxeter graph is B = [2, -1; -1, -2]. The generating reflections are s_1 = [-1, 1; 0, 1] and s_2 = [1, 0; -1, -1]. We have (s_1 s_2)^k = (-1)^k [f_{2k+1}, f_{2k}; f_{2k}, f_{2k-1}] where f_0 = 0, f_1 = 1, and f_n = f_{n-1} + f_{n-2} so that f_n is the nth Fibonacci number. This is a sequence of elements in the mixed-sign Coxeter group is never the identity. Furthermore, we also have s_2(s_1 s_2)^k = [f_{2k+1}, f_{2k}; -f_{2k+2}, -f_{2k+1}]. Thus, we have a found matrix representations for every element in the mixed-sign Coxeter group in terms of Fibonacci numbers. Notice in particular that s_2(s_1 s_2)^k e_1 = [f_{2k+1}; -f_{2k+2}]. The roots of this reflection system are therefore We_1 = \{(-1)^k [f_{2k+1}; f_{2k}], [f_{2k+1}; -f_{2k+2}]\} and We_2 = \{(-1)^k [f_{2k}; f_{2k-1}], [f_{2k}; -f_{2k-1}]\}. Let w_1 = s_2, w_2 = s_1 s_2, w_3 = s_2 s_1 s_2, w_4 = (s_1 s_2)^2, \ldots above. This gives a sequence of words in the mixed-sign Coxeter group that grows in length. However, notice the orbit of e_1 under these elements does not remain in \Phi^+, this shows Proposition 3.12. Figure 3.10 shows seven roots of the A_2(-, +)[3] mixed-sign Coxeter system.
lean_notes: Exact closed-form Fibonacci matrix formula for (s_1 s_2)^k and root-orbit sign oscillation.

statement: The element s_i s_j has order m(i, j) when m(i, j) is finite and \delta_i \delta_j = 1. If m(i, j) = \infty or \delta_i \delta_j = -1 then the element s_i s_j has infinite order.
proof: Notice that (s_i s_j)(e_k) = e_k if k \ne i, j. Restricting the action of (s_i s_j) to the space \mathrm{Span}\{e_i, e_j\} amounts to one of the rank 2 examples which we examined in Section 3.1.

statement: Suppose that \Gamma is a connected mixed-sign Coxeter graph with at least one positive and one negative node. Then W(\Gamma) is infinite.
proof: If \Gamma is connected and contains a positive and negative node, there must exist a positive node i connected to a negative node j, then the element s_i s_j has infinite order.
lean_notes: Proved in full generality for any connected ReflectionSystem with both a positive and a negative node.

statement: If (W, S, B) is a mixed-sign Coxeter group, then W is the quotient of a classical Coxeter group.
proof: Suppose that (W, S, B) has associated mixed-sign Coxeter graph \Gamma. We will define a classical Coxeter graph \hat{\Gamma} from \Gamma by so that \hat{\Gamma} has the same number of nodes as \Gamma. Let \hat{r}_i be a node in \hat{\Gamma}. The node \hat{r}_i corresponds to r_i \in \Gamma. Two nodes \hat{r}_i and \hat{r}_j are connected by an edge with weight \infty when r_i and r_j are connected in \Gamma. If r_i and r_j are not connected then \hat{r}_i and \hat{r}_j are not connected in \hat{\Gamma}. Then the mixed-sign Coxeter group W(\Gamma) is a quotient of the classical Coxeter group associated to W(\hat{\Gamma}). There is nothing special about this choice of \hat{\Gamma} there are other classical Coxeter groups which would also suffice to prove the statement. For instance, every rank n mixed-sign Coxeter group and classical Coxeter group is a quotient group of W(K_n[\infty]) where K_n[\infty] is the classical Coxeter graph which is a complete graph with n nodes and every edge weight has label \infty.

section: 3.3 The Deletion Property and proof of Theorem 1.2
proof: Consider the mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_{-2} in Figure 3.11. The mixed-sign Coxeter group is generated by three generators. W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}):= \langle s_1, s_2, s_3 \rangle. We think of these as the matrices s_1:= [-1, -1, -1; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1], s_2:= [1, 0, 0; -1, -1, -1; 0, 0, 1], s_3:= [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; -1, -1, -1]. By Lemma 3.17 we know that the group must have the relations s_1^2 = s_2^2 = s_3^2 = (s_1 s_2)^3 = (s_2 s_3)^3 = (s_1 s_3)^3 = 1. (3.21.1) Working towards a contradiction, assume that W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) only has the relations in 3.21.1, a group with only these relations would then have infinite order. Then W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) has infinite order. A computation of the matrices shows that we also have the relation (s_1 s_2 s_3)^4 = 1. (3.21.2) Again, assuming (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-2})) has the Deletion Property then the relation 3.21.2 must be a consequence of 3.21.1. However, the computer software GAP [GAP08] gives an isomorphism to the permutation group S_4: W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) \cong S_4 = \langle (1, 2), (1, 3), (1, 4) \rangle via S_4 \rightarrow W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}), (1, 2) \mapsto [-1, -1, -1; 0, 1, 0; 0, 0, 1] = s_1, (1, 3) \mapsto [1, 0, 0; -1, -1, -1; 0, 0, 1] = s_2, (1, 4) \mapsto [1, 0, 0; 0, 1, 0; -1, -1, -1] = s_3. Since S_4 is a finite group and S_4 \cong W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) therefore we conclude W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) is finite. This makes it impossible for the relation 3.21.2 to be a consequence of 3.21.1.

statement: The \widetilde{A}_n mixed-sign Coxeter graph is the cycle consisting of n + 1 positive nodes. The \widetilde{A}_{-n} mixed-sign Coxeter graph is the cycle consisting of n + 1 negative nodes. Notice that a graph is not bipartite exactly when the graph contains an even cycle. The mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_n where n is even is therefore not bipartite. We show that (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_n)) is not conjugate to (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-n})). Furthermore we justify our claim n = 2, 4, 6 \widetilde{A}_{-(n)} the mixed-sign Coxeter graph associates to a group which is finite and is isomorphic to finite classical Coxeter group W(D_{n+1}). The GAP [GAP08] code for the n = 4 case is in the appendix, see section D. In [Hum90] it is shown for every n that the \widetilde{A}_n associates to a classical Coxeter system; the bilinear forms are positive semi-definite and the associated reflection groups have infinite order. proof: We apply Lemma 3.17 on the mixed-sign Coxeter graph \widetilde{A}_2 in Figure 3.13. Since the \widetilde{A}_2 graph is a classical Coxeter graph, then we conclude that the group has the presentation W(\widetilde{A}_2) = \langle s_1, s_2, s_3 \mid s_1^2 = s_2^2 = s_3^2 = (s_1 s_2)^3 = (s_2 s_3)^3 = (s_1 s_3)^3 = 1 \rangle. As we indicated in the proof of Lemma 3.21 the group W(\widetilde{A}_2) has infinite order. Whereas, above, we found the group W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) has finite order.

statement: In Lemma 3.21 we show that (W, S, B(\widetilde{A}_{-2})) does not satisfy the Deletion Property. In doing so, we also show that W(\widetilde{A}_{-2}) is a finite order group whereas W(\widetilde{A}_2) is an infinite order group. We further remark that W(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) when n = 4 and n = 6 also has finite order. Again, we use the computer algebra system GAP [GAP08] to determine that the orders are 1920 and 322560, respectively. This implies that the groups are finite reflection groups. From standard Coxeter theory, the only Coxeter groups with these orders correspond to the D_5 and D_7 classical Coxeter graphs in A.1. Appendix D contains GAP code which shows explicitly shows the isomorphism between W(\widetilde{A}_{-4}) and W(D_5). We conjecture that if n is even then W(\widetilde{A}_n) has finite order and W(\widetilde{A}_{-n}) is isomorphic to W(D_{n+1}) where D_n is the classical Coxeter graph in Table A.1.

statement: Suppose w is a Coxeter element in a classical Coxeter group W then: If w has eigenvalues of modulus 1, and 1 is not an eigenvalue then the Coxeter system is spherical; If w has eigenvalues of modulus 1 and 1 is an eigenvalue then the Coxeter system is affine; If w has eigenvalues which are greater than 1 then the Coxeter system is hyperbolic or higher-rank. Furthermore, the eigenvalue of the graph of a classical Coxeter system is directly related to the spectral radius of Coxeter elements. Let \Gamma_1 and \Gamma_2 be two classical Coxeter graphs. We say that \Gamma_1 \subset \Gamma_2 if there is a map \varphi: \Gamma_1 \rightarrow \Gamma_2 such that \varphi: Nodes(\Gamma_1) \rightarrow Nodes(\Gamma_2) is injective; m(i, j) = m(\varphi(i), \varphi(j)) when \varphi(i) and \varphi(j) are defined.
lean_notes: Full spectral trichotomy (spherical / affine / indefinite) proved for bipartite classical Coxeter elements; see also SpectralRadius.lean (theorem_3_27_bipartite_coxeter_eigenvalue).

statement: (Interlacing Theorem for classical Coxeter graphs) Suppose \Gamma is a classical Coxeter graph and w_1 is a Coxeter element of W(\Gamma). Suppose r_i \in Node\Gamma and w_2 is a Coxeter element of W(\Gamma/(r_i)) then \lambda(w_1) > \lambda(w_2).
proof: The result follows from the standard interlacing theorem for graphs or positive matrices see [MS05] and [McM02].

statement: Consider the A_3(+, +, -) mixed-sign Coxeter graph in Figure 3.14. The mixed-sign Coxeter graph A_3(+, +, -) has an associated bilinear form B = [2, -1, 0; -1, 2, -1; 0, -1, -2] which has signature (2, 1, 0). Therefore, A_3(+, +, -) is a hyperbolic mixed-sign Coxeter graph. The spectral radius of a principal element in the A_3(+, +, -) system is 1. This indicates that the method of using the spectral radius of a principal element given by [A'C76] in Theorem 3.27, will not extend to the mixed-sign case. Furthermore, recall the A_2(+, -) mixed-sign Coxeter graph in Figure 3.9. Notice that, A_2(+, -) \subset A_3(+, +, -). After some computations we find \chi(A_2(+, -), x) = x^2 + 3x + 1 and \chi(A_3(+, +, -), x) = x^3 + 3x^2 + 3x + 1 and we notice 1 = \Lambda(A_3(+, +, -)) < \Lambda(A_2(+, -)) = (3 + \sqrt{5})/2 \approx 2.618 so Theorem 3.28 also fails to extend to mixed-sign Coxeter systems.
